Many have read Heidegger's remarks on our relations to things as saying that human beings are immersed in the world through language and everyday practices. This perspective suggests, on the one hand, that we cannot break through or extricate ourselves from our emplacement so as to get at things from the "outside," as it were, and, on the other hand, that the things of the world are never trumped by language or ideas. Our holistic entanglements are material and practical first and foremost. Hubert Dreyfus is a well-known proponent of this position and posits Heidegger as a "robust realist," meaning that Heidegger avoids the Scylla ofnaive realism and the Charybdis of idealism ("Coping" n.p.). The world is a participant in the ongoing event of human being-in-the-world, not a stage or backdrop to what human beings do and say. And this is a nuanced participation, with things emerging from and participating in human practices, and human practices in turn requiring things. Such an interpretation is fine as a first take, except that it exhibits a certain skewing: the nexus remains tethered to human being. Human usage and behavior become the privileged means of access to the background, and things, such as tools, light up to our awareness as we use them; then, when our attention shifts elsewhere, they dim back into the shadowy realm of equipment (Zeug) in general, the undifferentiated, always receding backdrop of"stuff."1 Heidegger certainly lends himself to such a reading. Speaking ofa room, he remarks that we encounter it not as a geometrical space but as "equipment for residingp that we have at least discovered, and that discovery and our activities yield

an arrangement that allows individual items to show themselves (BT 98). I take the steps downstairs into the basement, set out my books, organize my papers, boot the laptop, put some Klaus Schulze on the turntable, sit on the chair at the desk, insert the pen drive, enter words into the chapter file (i.e., write), read, take notes, edit, save the file, put on some Dexter Gordon. adjust the stereo volume, and so forth, with aspects of the room now near and now far from my attentions and activities. In various ways, these things all go together; there is an arrangement from which individual entities already derive their place wherefrom I can weave them through my activities. Entities in turn show up and dim back into the recesses as my attention flows variously through my purposeful activity.

In Tool-Being Graham Harman argues that such readings, reminiscent of Dreyfus, are not wrong but nevertheless miss something crucial to the nature of equipment and objects. Objects can no more be positioned solely within the horizon of human intention or awareness than language can. My example of the basement illustrates this tendency, since everything has its "nearness" and "farness" in relation to my attentions and intentions. One could of course add more history here and pile on thick description across the attentions and intentions of other people, social roles, and equipment. But none of this suffices to give us any ultimate grip on the object. Harman argues that "ifwe could total up all the 'contexts, roles, and social goals' in which a specific bridge or flagpole are currently embedded, this would still not give us the being of these objects" (TB 124). Any use or meaning that I or anyone else can bring, or even the plenitude of people, uses, contexts, histories, and other objects that could be brought forward, only serves to present some particular qualities out of the object's fulsomeness, or what Harman calls its "grand, dark abundance" (TB 125). Indeed. as the new wave of cognitive science (such as the work of Andy Clark, Paul Dourish, Anthony Chemero, and so on) demonstrates, the use of tools and local environmental scaffolding inspires changes in our sense of embodiment, blurring boundaries; to use a computer mouse, for instance, amounts to making that mouse part of one's body, and in so doing, it effectively disappears.8 Thus, predicating ontological distinctions on human attention and its shifting cognitive and bodily boundaries is fruitless; the ontological has to manifest beyond such human-derived loci, and thus withdrawal does not depend on human perception or any other singular interaction.

Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Paper need not know the meaning of fire in order to burn. But in the "idea" offire there is a persuasive ingredient. By this route something of the rhetorical motive comes to lurk in every "meaning" however purely "scientific" its pretensions. Wherever there is persuasion, there is rhetoric. And wherever there is "meaning," there is "persuasion." Food, eaten and digested, is not rhetorical. But in the meaning o[food there is much rhetoric, the meaning being persuasive enough for the idea of food to be used, like the ideas ofreligion, as a rhetorical device of statesmen. (RM 172-73)

This passage seems far from clear. Additionally, the numerous ironizing quotation marks and italics indicate various forms of pressure and stress. The word meaning, not insignificantly, is italicized twice and twice placed in quotation marks. What does meaning mean here? The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. Meaning is gleaned from the symbolicity that drapes over (or maybe permeates) the mundane world, circulating it as the significance available to us. The mention of science is important here, for Burke is clearly dissatisfied with a positivist, scientific claim of mere facticity for things of the world, as if measuring qualia sufficed for generating meaning. Thus, he will grant that paper, being paper, has no ideas as such; its rapid oxidation at temperatures around 451 degrees Fahrenheit is a purely chemical reaction. But to remain at this level is to willfully (or methodologically) remain at observation degree zero, and it obscures fire's role in human affairs. When Bradbury's Fireman comes to

burn the books, though, we move into a different realm, one of meaning, and we see that fire is a full rhetorical participant. Fire, then, is more than just a sensed material phenomenon; its integration into the human world necessitates ideas. These ideas mean, and insofar as they mean, they bodily invoke, and insofar as they bodily invoke, they persuade.

As I observed in my discussion of Hawhee, this is not an abstract notion of fire as meaningful; rather, it is one entirely grounded in the bodily integration of ideas stemming from physical experience. As Burke puts it in Attitudes toward History, "our primeval ancestors, by learning language, no longer experienced a sensation solely as a sensation" (382). As he goes on to explain, we may like the warmth ofa fire, and such warmth is certainly a sensation, but as soon as we start putting such experience into language, the words come to "tell a story"; as a result, attitudes (or affective stances) can emerge and be deployed across various forms of discursive interaction, such as the movement from "that feels warm" to the observation that someone is "warm-hearted" (Burke,AH383).

This elevation of meaning over mundane, objective matter is further evinced in other passages. Later in A Rhetoric of Motives Burke again discusses the effect of material phenomena. This time he calls them a form of intuition, and he then tethers intuition to a notion of infancy. Empedocles and Heidegger continually emphasized the need to forge a positive way forward, to work not just with who people are but with where they are. We cannot escape the infrastructures, industries, and lifeways people currently have but must work within and through them towards a more ecologically attuned dwelling. In this regard, science, technology, and capitalism will need to become part of that path, despite the fact that these are some of the most common targets for environmentalist critique. On these points I take inspiration from Peter Sloterdijk's digression on spaceships in his massive philosophical trilogy, Spheres. Sloterdijk argues that spaceships are more than technological objects—they are equally ontological interventions. The suturing

of a thing to ontology harkens back to Heidegger, and we can see how Sloterdijk's spaceship updates Heidegger's jugs and bridges. But there is also an inversion: jugs and bridges evoke an interconnected whole to which we are all wedded and indebted; a spaceship, however, operates in a realm of extreme inhospitality. Space is nonconductive for nearly all life as we know it. Since no aspect of dwelling in space can be taken for granted, a spaceship "constitutes a world model," a kind of "immanence machine."73 The level of explicatory detail necessary for surviving in such a harsh environment is vertiginous. To give one small example: astronauts must sleep with fans next to them, less their exhalations, which do not move in zero gravity, suffocate them in a bubble of nitrogen and carbon dioxide.74 There is no resting on unexplicated assumptions, as is possible back on Earth where the ecological background can simply be assumed, as Moore exemplifed through capitalism's cavalier appropriations of nature. Space lacks such "ontological comfort."75

The point, Sloterdijk argues, is that "space travel amounts to an ontological alphabetization: what follows from it is that the elements of being-in-the-world can, and must, be written."76 Sloterdijk picks up the thread we saw connecting Empedocles and Aristotle in the movement from roots to elements, where increasing abstraction and alphabetization formalize as science and episteme. Sloterdijk also counters Abram's argument that abstraction goes hand in hand with the West's loss of intimacy with the environment. Rather, Sloterdijk taps a great affrmation resonant with Empedocles and Heidegger. It is the affrmation of the fourfold. The lesson is that abstraction and alphabetization also gather the fourfold and disclose the worldly depths of rich interconnection. Spaceships necessitate this insight. For life to maintain itself in space, bubbles of lifeworld must be constructed. To construct a bubble of lifeworld requires a profoundly rich explication of an ecological background we take for granted on earth, where our lifeworld is simply given. For spacecraft, these ABCs of lifeworlding must be spelled out and implemented through the technics of disclosure and building. As Heidegger has argued, to build is to dwell, and here we see how this manifests in even the most focused technological enterprise.77

The explicative disclosure necessary for space travel thus affrms some of environmentalism's biggest demons—abstraction, science, technology, capitalist progress. In terms of an ambient rhetoric, we must not simply turn our sights to sound and ask how we can now use sound to generate desired affective responses. As I stated earlier, we need more than a sonic semiotic. That would certainly be a possibility, but it obscures the deeper insights that sonics thought ambiently can afford us. We can do more with this insight into the ambience of design than single out and focus on various strands, such as the functional (how usable it is), the cognitive (what it means for us), or the affective (how it makes us feel). Instead, we could build a fresh, cumulative list of things with which we might concern ourselves as teachers, writers, and rhetoricians. I have argued that it is better to see them as complexly generating an overarching ambient environment that cradles, without forcing, particular affective responses or that fosters an attunement (as with "clear, confident, and connected," which is Microsoft's take on a positive, secure feeling that will enable work and play). Such a perspective reflects a fuller, less instrumental view of human beings and their interactions, particularly multimedia rhetorics. It deprivileges dir ectly conscious experience and boosts the importance of indirect, unconscious, auratic, osmotic, and ambient phenomena. Put differently, such rhet orical design

organizes an experience, not so much to persuade in any direct sense, but to attune and inflect our sense of bodily inhabitance and the cradle of intelligibility within which we comport ourselves. It is worth recalling Eno's irony-laden dismissal of the corporate sloganeering Microsoft delivered to him as part of the project. If Microsoft perhaps intended more direct forms of marketing and the shaping of the user's experience, including the service of avant-garde musicians to brand Microsoft products, it is important that Eno's music resists such narrowing. For Eno, ambient music is inherently political, evoking new senses of place and how human beings inhabit it; this includes, more pointedly, a reduced role for human agency reflecting a more distributed, ecological approach to will, action, and consequence. The lengthy video session with Robert Fripp and the Microsoft team suggests that such aesthetics and their politics, however indirect, are nevertheless in play. So, while startup music itself makes up only a small element amid these far larger concerns (not to mention the larger expanse of sonic space and its rhetorical-architectural possibilities), possibly one of little relevance, it nevertheless can open us onto a deeper reflection concerning our relation to technology, space, and sonics, and we lose much ifwe ignore the insights it grants.

There is thus another dimension to persuasion that is as fundamental as the issue Davis hosts for us. Sociality resides. It is always somewhere, and this somewhere can never be fully circumscribed by either meaning or symbolicity. We are worldly. Necessarily, our a priori affectability is not just a transaction among animate beings-humans primarily, but as Davis suggests, also nonhuman animals-so that we see this affectability as enmeshed in material locales that give place and bearing prior to symbolicity proper. All being must be part of the giving of what gives, and the world is what is given, both as meaning and as what withdraws from meaning, even ifworld is not equivalently given. Thus, the challenge of this chapter is to think how rhetoric is caught up in the play of language and materiality while raising the specter that neither language nor materiality can be reduced to symbolicity. Indeed, that is the problem: to what extent can we discuss materiality prior to meaning or symbolicity, and how can we discuss what gives rise to symbolicity as part of symbolicity itself? These questions are themselves problematic from Burke's perspective. Burke almost uniformly places meaning first, and the rhetoricity implicit to symbolic action emerges with it. Heidegger, too, can be and frequently has been read as offering this position, which thus has been taken to mean that world, while certainly material, is always already and only one of significance, making

world inseparable from meaning. I, however, am going to argue that while the world is a world of involvements, and hence meaning, world is also involved in those involvements in ways that are never captured, submerged, or rendered secondary to world as it emerges for human being. This sense of world requires a rich materiality that bears up and stays within human sociality and significance, so that it must also be understood as constituting affective relationality, without, for all that, collapsing into human sociality and significance. Such materiality, as I will show in the upcoming chapters, should always be understood across the play of presence and withdrawal, and human being is only one locus for this play.

When I claim rhetoric is ontological, then, I mean that (1) we come to see that rhetoric cannot be sundered from material being or reduced to epistemological considerations; (2) we understand that rhetoric is intimate with the environments in which it emerges (and not just to which it is joined, as in two separate realms coming together), which grants non humans an elemental role in rhetoricity; (3) this intimacy is not solely a matter of human projection, control. or assignment; and (4) grappling with these entangled, mutually coevolving, and transformative interactions among persons, world, and discourses requires a new appreciation for their constitutive complexity. I can reduce this to a somewhat more succinct statement: rhetoric is a responsive way of revealing the world for others, responding to and put forth through affective, symbolic, and material means, so as to (at least potentially) reattune or otherwise transform how others inhabit the world to an extent that calls for some action (which can include, of course, steadfastness, refusal, or even apathy). Beyond resonating with Davis's approach, my line of thought also bears an affinity to George Kennedy's important essay "A Hoot in the Dark," where Kennedy claims that rhetoric is energy (2). I augment Kennedy, however, by adding that energy is always materialized. Energy emerges within and transforms how one dwells in the world or at least allows for that world to show up, to reveal itself, differently. Ifwe are going to keep to persuasion, then, this is a further intensification of it. Persuasion thought ambiently looks to a materialist affectability that sustains our being-in-the-world. An ambient rhetoric will have taken things at their world and notjust their word.

To take one instance, speakers or writers may well understand themselves as working with conscious intent, yet the intention may be causally irrelevant to the effects produced in the audience. Rhetorical theory tends to assume that intent equals result: a rhetor wants to persuade a group of people to vote a certain way, the rhetor succeeds, and therefore the rhetor's intent is held to have been successfully realized through his or her rhetorical art. Arabella Lyon remarks that rhetoric has maintained its boundaries by this adherence to discourse understood as instrumental (4). This is also rhetoric's built-in retroactivity, according to which what works is always telegraphed by an initial intentional action. Curiously, however, intent is rarely called into question when a rhetorical message goes awry; rather, the issue becomes a matter of technique. This idea underpins the longstanding idea of rhetoric as a teachable art. Failure results because one's message was not sufficient for the intent, because one was unprepared for the pa rticular audience, because one made a mistake, and so on. There is no leeway for accidental persuasion, for persuasion at odds with or in spite of intent or even the artistry of rhetorical work. Instead, the causality of rhetorical intent actualized through rhetorical work is often assumed as an unquestionable given. A great deal of excellent work, however, has been done on aleatory methods (see Vitanza, "From Heuristic"); unconscious forms of persuasion, such as Burke's identification, taken from psychoanalysis (see D. Davis, Inessential; Lundberg and Gunn); complexity and ecology (Cooper, Dobrin, Edbauer, Hawk, Lanham); and various proponents of hermeneutic and postmodern thought (Biesecker; Hyde; Lyon; Mailloux, "Rhetorical Hermeneutics" and "Rhetorical Hermeneutics Still"). It is

thus perhaps surprising that we have not made more progress here. But as Lyon suggests, intent has in fact been woefully undertheorized in rhetoric precisely because it is always assumed (3-4). What I have described as essential to an ambient rhetoric-its embodied and embedded or situated character, its dispersal across things that themselves have gradations of agency, and its dynamic emergence within an environment that occasions certain effects-suggests that intent is only one element in a large array of things, feelings, peoples, and forces all complexly interacting. To say this is not to deny the existence or importance of intent but rather to insist that within any given rhetorical event, intent cannot suffice for its full accounting as rhetoric-not to mention the near dogmatic assertion of intent as the expression of the subjective will.

The emphasis on self-consciousness, another aspect of Cole's definition, is just as problematic. Each of the four strands of thought I brought to the notion of ambient rhetoric emphasizes the idea that at any given time, we are only partially conscious of what we are doing, why we are doing it, and what will result from it. When we tether intent to self-consciousness, we cut off large swaths of human activity from rhetorical practice in our rhetorical theory. That last prepositional phrase is crucial: the point is not that what is denied to self-consciousness fails to come into play in rhetorical engagement but that we deny inquiry into those aspects when our rhetorical theory opens itself only onto what is immediately self-conscious and thus easily tethered to humanist notions of willing. Intent and selfconsciousness no doubt matter enormously, but they no longer suffice to determine what rhetoric is and is not. Behind the conventional notion of intention lies a model of human being as an autonomous, self-knowing, subjective agent. Everything I have here described works to undo and disperse this model as a reduced view of human being.

In sum, I hope this book helps us to see such narrowing as a way to impoverish rhetoric when we should be opening it up, not to make it bigger, but to attune us, in rhetoric and via rhetoric, to its fullest flowering. Rhetoric's timeliness as a field of inquiry and a practice has never been more propitious. As I suggested previously, transformations in ourselves, in our historical conjuncture, and in our built environments have occasioned revised understandings of human being and the world. The dynamically ecological imbrications of places, things, and informatics can be read as a (partial) rhetoricization of the world in the most concrete and material way imaginable. Its presence in our lives will transfigure our notions of space and time, self and other, citizen and society in ways we haven't begun to contemplate" (3). In short, ambient intelligence radically changes who we are in our environs; it

situates us differently in the world, evoking other ways of being. It thereby also reveals rhetoric to us differently than it has appeared heretofore. Ambience thus teaches us that we cannot rely solely on salience, attention, and consciousness to guide us.

Rhetoric has much to learn from music on this score. I am claiming that ambient music is an important development, both in its own right as a form of thinking (and not simply as expression ofhuman thought and affect) and as something that shows how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to the music's creation but to what we take the music to be. Music is not just the salience of its affective work. Ambient music has still other rhetorical dimensions, including politics. It has ramifications for how we dwell in the world. Eno claims that ambient music is directly political: "The decision to stop seeing yourself as the centre of the world, to see yourself as part of the greater flow of things, as having limited options and responsibility for your actions[.] ... that is political theory: and it's where the music grows from" (qtd. in Tamm 91).

It is hardly a stretch to see that these political insights resonate with the extension of digital computing into things and environs. As Eno is quite aware, there are both opportunities and dangers here, which is why transforming how one sees oneself in the world is integral to a politics attuned to these dangers. 21 So, much as ambient music does, ubiquitous computing (ambient intelligence) showcases how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to our everyday activity but to a conception of dynamic life itself. We need not overstate the case by claiming we are on the threshold of a brave new world. Rather, we are simply seeing capacities, implications, and energies as previously assembled now giving way to vibrant and different intensities and assemblages. But we cannot ignore how these different forms also assemble new forms oflife, or new ways of being-in-the-world.

Rhetoric, Ambience, Dwelling

We need conceptions ofrhetoric that keep pace with these transformations and their attendant opportunities and dangers, that not only help us make sense of them but enable us to flourish (and that will, of course, spur new transformations). We do not need a new rhetoric, however; rather, we must work anew with what has been brought forward in rhetorical theory and practice.
